prize_parts.citation: For transforming the measurement of intergenerational mobility with population-scale administrative data, and for developing designs that separate the causal effects of childhood environment and place from family sorting.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is still B002, with the same three names. The reason is that the contribution joins a new empirical object to explanatory designs. Linking population-scale administrative records made intergenerational mobility observable at fine geographic resolution. Movers and childhood-exposure designs then separated causal place effects from family sorting. In my view that combination of data discovery and a framework that explains the patterns is what the prize rewards. The contribution is also checkable. The designs are transparent, and national register data, including Swedish data, allow outside researchers to test them. After the exchange I have narrowed the citation. It now credits the measurement advance and the exposure-based designs, and it makes no claim about long-run policy conclusions or the full size of causal place effects. That answers the maturity objection from Strömberg, Krusell, Enflo and the chair at the level of what is best established, without discounting the work for being under a decade old. I am not relying on opening support counts. The shared trio in the openings only shows that colleagues read the attribution similarly, and it is not evidence of merit. The attribution is tractable, with Chetty, Hendren and Friedman as the closest unit on the mobility and place-effects papers.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations are maturity and the Katz question, and I take both more seriously than in round 1. On maturity, the core results are from about 2014 to 2022. The size and long-run interpretation of causal place effects are still debated, and specific small-area estimates are noisy. A committee that wants a longer confirmation record, as the B015 and B027 supporters do, is applying a legitimate criterion. On Katz, my round-1 framing of Moving to Opportunity as an input to the neighbourhood-effects question understated his role. From general knowledge, not independent verification, the long-run reanalysis of that experiment was a joint project of Chetty, Hendren and Katz, so Katz's claim rests on more than a single experiment. The seat I find genuinely contestable is Friedman versus Katz. Which of them belongs in the trio depends on whether the citation stresses data-infrastructure and mobility atlas work (Friedman) or the experimental evidence on exposure (Katz). A further concern is that a part for administrative-data measurement may be read as primarily empirical rather than conceptual. If the committee holds that view, B002 should wait.

responses.point: Boppart said Moving to Opportunity is an input to the causal neighbourhood-effects question, that the reanalysis was done by the Chetty-Hendren-Friedman group, and that if the Katz argument is decisive the alternative is a different trio, which would displace one of the three names.
responses.response: You asked which name an argument for Katz would displace. My answer is Friedman, and I do not think the call is obvious. I also need to correct my own earlier framing and your description of the reanalysis. As I recall it, the long-run Moving to Opportunity work was by Chetty, Hendren and Katz, not by the Friedman group, so Katz's claim is stronger than I first allowed. I still keep Friedman, because the citation I propose rests on two things: the population-scale measurement of mobility, and designs separating place effects from sorting. Friedman is tied to the tax-record data construction and the place-level mobility estimates in the first of these. If the Committee wanted a citation built around the experimental and quasi-experimental exposure evidence, the Chetty-Hendren-Katz trio would be the better fit. I would want that tabled as a separate configuration and compared on the evidence, with no assumption that it is the same discovery.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B002 seventh and said the risk is that the findings prove data-driven rather than foundational and that causal neighbourhood effects are contested. He prefers B015, and he argues that a younger programme with a contested causal reading is a smaller risk than diffuse credit across eight names.
responses.response: You and I agree on the trade-off. Maturity is the real cost of B002 and attribution is the real cost of B015, and neither disappears. I weigh them differently, because a prize can be written around what is already well established. The measurement standard and the designs that separate place effects from selection are already used with other national registers. I give that more weight than contested point estimates. A B015 citation can be written narrowly as well, but the cap cannot be fixed by wording. The Committee must still exclude Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler, and the exclusion is not obviously principled. You say yourself that this is the one case where the cap may do real injustice. I do not think B002 has an equivalent problem, though the Friedman and Katz seat is a real question. I take your originators-versus-developers distinction as serious, and I have not tried to settle B015 on its merits here.

responses.point: Teorell separates the 2024 institutions prize, which concerns the origins of institutions and prosperity, from B027, which treats institutions as given and asks how electoral rules and state capacity shape policy. He accepts that identification is weaker than in design-based work and rates B002 second for that reason.
responses.response: Your distinction from the 2024 prize is persuasive to me, and it moves me. In round 1 I treated that proximity as a real boundary problem for B027. I now think it is mainly a timing consideration and not a scientific objection, since the content differs. My remaining preference for B002 does not rest on the 2024 overlap. It rests on the identification point, which you accept. The mobility and exposure claims come from designs that others can examine directly. That is why B027 stays my alternative and not my first choice. I would not object to a Persson-Tabellini-Besley prize on grounds of novelty. I also note your point that Besley's work on state capacity and political selection is a separate strand, and I would not cut the trio to a pair merely to simplify the attribution.

responses.point: Strömberg replied to my criticism that the aggregate evidence for B004 is indirect. He said the pledgeable-collateral logic has been examined in firm and household credit studies, and that he would credit Gertler only for the intermediary-finance strand.
responses.response: That reply narrows my disagreement, and I accept that the evidence for the underlying logic is cumulative and varied in design, not just calibrated. I still do not move B004 into my top group. The aggregate claims are what the macro prize would credit, and the marginal novelty relative to 2022 is hard for me to judge. I also agree with you and Hassler that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clean originators. If the Committee goes to B004, I would prefer the pair to a trio in which Gertler's credit cannot be separated from the accelerator. I would not oppose it, and I think it is a more tractable attribution problem than the B015 cut.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg supports the same trio for B002. She argues that checkability and transparent large-sample designs make it robust, that the durable part is the administrative-data standard, and that the citation should name both the measurement advance and the credible evidence on neighbourhood effects so the prize does not reward data access alone.
responses.response: I agree, and the revised citation follows that suggestion. I would add one caution to the robustness argument. Large samples reduce sampling noise but they do not remove identification risk. Movers designs depend on assumptions about whether the timing of moves is exogenous, and estimates for small areas can be noisy even with population data. For that reason I would not let the citation claim more than the exposure-based evidence supports, and I would leave policy conclusions out. On the point about data access alone, I still think the discovery is both data and design, and I would defend that reading in front of colleagues who regard it as only measurement.

uncertainties: Whether replication and extension of the exposure-effect estimates in non-US administrative data, and further long-run follow-up, are enough to settle the maturity concern. I think a citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs does not need the full long-run causal claims, but I cannot show that from the supplied files.
Whether the third seat should go to Friedman or to Katz. I now treat this as an open question that depends on whether the citation stresses data infrastructure or the experimental exposure evidence.
Whether the Committee would see the contribution as measurement more than as a conceptual advance, and whether it would prefer to wait.
Whether B024 or B027 is the better fallback. B024 was little discussed in the exchange, so I cannot say how colleagues would assess it, and its Katz credit overlaps with B002.
My assessments rest on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied files. I have not independently verified citations, replication results or authorship claims.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited B002 names is apparent from my supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. My work in labour economics, crime and administrative-data quasi-experiments is close to B002 and B024, and I have used Swedish register data. This closeness may make me favour design-based evidence, and I disclose it without adjudicating it. I joined the Committee in 2023 and presented the 2023 prize, which is a matter of public record and not a connection to any candidate. I note the other members' disclosures, including the Hassler-Krusell-Boppart-Friberg co-authorships, Persson's past committee service and field adjacency, and I treat them as disclosures only. They do not change how I weigh the evidence.
